Supervised Learning - Foundations Project: ReCell¶

Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

Buying and selling used phones and tablets used to be something that happened on a handful of online marketplace sites. But the used and refurbished device market has grown considerably over the past decade, and a new IDC (International Data Corporation) forecast predicts that the used phone market would be worth \$52.7bn by 2023 with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 13.6% from 2018 to 2023. This growth can be attributed to an uptick in demand for used phones and tablets that offer considerable savings compared with new models.

Refurbished and used devices continue to provide cost-effective alternatives to both consumers and businesses that are looking to save money when purchasing one. There are plenty of other benefits associated with the used device market. Used and refurbished devices can be sold with warranties and can also be insured with proof of purchase. Third-party vendors/platforms, such as Verizon, Amazon, etc., provide attractive offers to customers for refurbished devices. Maximizing the longevity of devices through second-hand trade also reduces their environmental impact and helps in recycling and reducing waste. The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak may further boost this segment as consumers cut back on discretionary spending and buy phones and tablets only for immediate needs.

Objective¶

The rising potential of this comparatively under-the-radar market fuels the need for an ML-based solution to develop a dynamic pricing strategy for used and refurbished devices. ReCell, a startup aiming to tap the potential in this market, has hired you as a data scientist. They want you to analyze the data provided and build a linear regression model to predict the price of a used phone/tablet and identify factors that significantly influence it.

Data Description¶

The data contains the different attributes of used/refurbished phones and tablets. The data was collected in the year 2021. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

  • brand_name: Name of manufacturing brand
  • os: OS on which the device runs
  • screen_size: Size of the screen in cm
  • 4g: Whether 4G is available or not
  • 5g: Whether 5G is available or not
  • main_camera_mp: Resolution of the rear camera in megapixels
  • selfie_camera_mp: Resolution of the front camera in megapixels
  • int_memory: Amount of internal memory (ROM) in GB
  • ram: Amount of RAM in GB
  • battery: Energy capacity of the device battery in mAh
  • weight: Weight of the device in grams
  • release_year: Year when the device model was released
  • days_used: Number of days the used/refurbished device has been used
  • normalized_new_price: Normalized price of a new device of the same model in euros
  • normalized_used_price: Normalized price of the used/refurbished device in euros

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

  • EDA is an important part of any project involving data.
  • It is important to investigate and understand the data better before building a model with it.
  • A few questions have been mentioned below which will help you approach the analysis in the right manner and generate insights from the data.
  • A thorough analysis of the data, in addition to the questions mentioned below, should be done.

Questions:

  1. What does the distribution of normalized used device prices look like?
  2. What percentage of the used device market is dominated by Android devices?
  3. The amount of RAM is important for the smooth functioning of a device. How does the amount of RAM vary with the brand?
  4. A large battery often increases a device's weight, making it feel uncomfortable in the hands. How does the weight vary for phones and tablets offering large batteries (more than 4500 mAh)?
  5. Bigger screens are desirable for entertainment purposes as they offer a better viewing experience. How many phones and tablets are available across different brands with a screen size larger than 6 inches?
  6. A lot of devices nowadays offer great selfie cameras, allowing us to capture our favorite moments with loved ones. What is the distribution of devices offering greater than 8MP selfie cameras across brands?
  7. Which attributes are highly correlated with the normalized price of a used device?

# Calculate the market share of each operating system
os_counts = df['os'].value_counts()
os_market_share = (os_counts / os_counts.sum()) * 100

# Create a DataFrame for plotting

# Sort the data by market share for better visualization

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))

plt.title('Used Device Market Share by Operating System')

plt.ylabel('Market Share (%)')
plt.ylim(0, 100)
plt.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)

plt.show()

# Define the conversion factor and the threshold for 6 inches in centimeters
inches_to_cm = 2.54
six_in_cm = 6 * inches_to_cm

big_screen = df[df['screen_size'] > six_in_cm]

counts = (big_screen
          .groupby(['brand_name','device_type'])
          .size()
          .reset_index(name='count')
          .sort_values(['device_type','count'], ascending=[True, False]))
print(counts.head(30))

# Pivot for readability

plot_df = counts[counts['brand_name'].isin(top_brands)]

plot_df.loc[top_brands].plot(kind='bar', stacked=True, figsize=(9,5), colormap='tab20')
plt.title('Devices > 6 inches by brand and type')

# Prepare numeric features (including binary 4g/5g)
feat_cols = ['screen_size','main_camera_mp','selfie_camera_mp','int_memory','ram','battery','weight',
             'release_year','days_used','normalized_new_price','4g','5g']
corr = df[feat_cols + ['normalized_used_price']].corr(numeric_only=True)

target_corr = corr['normalized_used_price'].drop('normalized_used_price').sort_values(key=np.abs, ascending=False)
print('Correlation with normalized_used_price:')
print(target_corr.round(3))

plt.figure(figsize=(6,8))
sns.heatmap(target_corr.to_frame(), annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='coolwarm', vmin=-1, vmax=1, cbar=False)
plt.title('Feature correlation with used price')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Optional: multicollinearity view

sns.heatmap(corr, cmap='coolwarm', vmin=-1, vmax=1, annot=False)

plt.tight_layout()

Outlier Check¶

. Let's check for outliers in the data.

In [21]:
# List of numerical columns to check for outliers
numerical_cols = df.select_dtypes(include=np.number).columns.tolist()

# Exclude the target variable and year_since_release from outlier check as they represent time or target
# and outliers might be meaningful data points
cols_to_check_outliers = [col for col in numerical_cols if col not in ['normalized_used_price', 'release_year', 'years_since_release']]


for col in cols_to_check_outliers:
    Q1 = df[col].quantile(0.25)
    Q3 = df[col].quantile(0.75)
    IQR = Q3 - Q1

    lower_bound = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
    upper_bound = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR

    outliers = df[(df[col] < lower_bound) | (df[col] > upper_bound)]

    print(f"Outliers for column '{col}':")
    print(outliers.shape[0]) # Print the number of outliers
    # Optionally, display the outlier rows for inspection:
    # display(outliers)

Data Preparation for modeling¶

  • We want to predict the normalized price of used devices
  • Before we proceed to build a model, we'll have to encode categorical features
  • We'll split the data into train and test to be able to evaluate the model that we build on the train data
  • We will build a Linear Regression model using the train data and then check it's performance

Model Performance Check¶

Let's check the performance of the model using different metrics.

In [56]:
# function to compute adjusted R-squared
def adj_r2_score(predictors, targets, predictions):
    r2 = r2_score(targets, predictions)
    n = predictors.shape[0]
    k = predictors.shape[1]
    return 1 - ((1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1))


# function to compute MAPE
def mape_score(targets, predictions):
    return np.mean(np.abs(targets - predictions) / targets) * 100


# function to compute different metrics to check performance of a regression model
def model_performance_regression(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check regression model performance

    model: regressor
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """
    # Add a constant to the predictors if it's not already present
    predictors = sm.add_constant(predictors, has_constant='add')


    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    r2 = r2_score(target, pred)  # to compute R-squared
    adjr2 = adj_r2_score(predictors, target, pred)  # to compute adjusted R-squared
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(target, pred))  # to compute RMSE
    mae = mean_absolute_error(target, pred)  # to compute MAE
    mape = mape_score(target, pred)  # to compute MAPE

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "RMSE": rmse,
            "MAE": mae,
            "R-squared": r2,
            "Adj. R-squared": adjr2,
            "MAPE": mape,
        },
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf

The Shapiro-Wilk test can also be used for checking the normality. The null and alternate hypotheses of the test are as follows:

  • Null hypothesis - Data is normally distributed.
  • Alternate hypothesis - Data is not normally distributed.

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

  1. New price is the strongest driver of used price
. A unit increase in normalized new price raises used price by 0.42 units.
. This confirms that resale markets are anchored around the original launch price.

2. Hardware specs matter significantly

. RAM (0.032, p < 0.001) and cameras (main + selfie) are strong contributors to higher resale value.
. Battery capacity is not significant, meaning buyers don’t value it as much once other specs are accounted for.
. Weight has a surprisingly strong positive effect, possibly acting as a proxy for build quality or premium design.

3. Device age reduces value

. Each additional year since release lowers resale value by 3.2% on average.
. Depreciation is real and consistent.

4. Connectivity features

. 4G support adds value, but 5G shows a negative coefficient (likely due to low-cost entry-level 5G phones dragging down resale values).

5. Brand influence is weaker than expected

. Only Celkon (significantly negative) and “Others” brands show consistent resale penalties.

. Big brands like Apple, Samsung, Huawei are not statistically significant once specs and new price are controlled.

6. Operating System

. Devices under “Other OS” are heavily discounted.

. iOS and Windows don’t show significant effects after accounting for specs and new price.

For Manufacturers & Retailers¶

Highlight premium specs (RAM, camera quality, build) in marketing since these sustain value in the secondary market.

Invest less in oversized batteries, as they don’t strongly influence resale value.

Avoid niche/alternative OS platforms — they depreciate faster.

For Resellers & Refurbishers¶

Use new price and years since release as core predictors for pricing models.

Bundle or promote devices with stronger RAM and cameras to increase resale appeal.

Be cautious with 5G devices — verify market demand, as not all 5G models retain value.

For Consumers¶

Buying tip: Premium RAM/camera phones hold their value better → good investment if planning to resell.

Selling tip: Sell devices earlier (before too many years pass), since depreciation accelerates with age.

Avoid minor brands if you care about resale value — they depreciate more quickly.

Convert data types¶

Subtask:¶

Convert relevant columns to appropriate numeric types, handling errors by coercing invalid values to NaN.

Reasoning: The error message ValueError: shapes (2417,50) and (2417,50) not aligned: 50 (dim 1) != 2417 (dim 0) in the previous cell indicates an issue with matrix multiplication within the statsmodels OLS prediction, likely due to a mismatch in the number of rows between the design matrix (X_train) and the coefficients (model.params). Although the shapes appear to match, the error suggests an internal misalignment. This could be caused by NaN values introduced during the conversion to numeric types in the previous steps, which were not handled before fitting the OLS model. The current subtask is to convert relevant columns to numeric types, coercing errors to NaN. I will apply pd.to_numeric to all columns in X_train and X_test to ensure they are numeric, as the error might stem from non-numeric values in the input to the sm.OLS model or the prediction step.

Split data¶

Subtask:¶

Split the preprocessed data into training and testing sets (e.g., 70:30 ratio).

Reasoning: The previous code block failed because the model_performance_regression function was not defined. This function is needed to evaluate the performance of the linear regression model. I need to define this function first. After defining the function, I will call it to evaluate the model performance on the training data.

In [80]:
# Function to calculate and print the performance metrics of the regression model
def model_performance_regression(model, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test):
    """
    Calculates and prints the performance metrics of a regression model.

    Args:
        model: The fitted regression model.
        X_train (pd.DataFrame): Training features.
        y_train (pd.Series): Training target.
        X_test (pd.DataFrame): Testing features.
        y_test (pd.Series): Testing target.
    """
    # Drop existing 'const' column to avoid duplicates before adding constant
    if 'const' in X_train.columns:
        X_train = X_train.drop('const', axis=1)
    if 'const' in X_test.columns:
        X_test = X_test.drop('const', axis=1)


    # Add constant to X_test if it's not already present
    X_test = sm.add_constant(X_test, has_constant='add')

    # Add constant to X_train
    X_train = sm.add_constant(X_train, has_constant='add')

    # Reindex X_test columns to match X_train columns
    X_test = X_test.reindex(columns=X_train.columns, fill_value=0)


    # Predicting on train and test set
    y_pred_train = model.predict(X_train)
    y_pred_test = model.predict(X_test)

    # R-squared
    r2_train = r2_score(y_train, y_pred_train)
    r2_test = r2_score(y_test, y_pred_test)

    # Adjusted R-squared (for train set only as test set typically uses R-squared)
    n_train = X_train.shape[0]
    p_train = X_train.shape[1] -1 # Subtracting 1 for the intercept
    adjusted_r2_train = 1 - (1 - r2_train) * (n_train - 1) / (n_train - p_train - 1)


    # MAE
    mae_train = mean_absolute_error(y_train, y_pred_train)
    mae_test = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred_test)

    # MSE
    mse_train = mean_squared_error(y_train, y_pred_train)
    mse_test = mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred_test)

    # RMSE
    rmse_train = np.sqrt(mse_train)
    rmse_test = np.sqrt(mse_test)

    # Creating a DataFrame to display the metrics
    metrics = pd.DataFrame({
        'Metric': ['R-squared', 'Adjusted R-squared', 'MAE', 'MSE', 'RMSE'],
        'Train': [r2_train, adjusted_r2_train, mae_train, mse_train, rmse_train],
        'Test': [r2_test, np.nan, mae_test, mse_test, rmse_test] # Adjusted R-squared is typically not reported for test set
    })
    print(metrics)

# print("Training Performance\n") # This call is outside the function definition
# olsmodel1_train_perf = model_performance_regression(olsmodel1, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test) # This call is outside the function definition

Reasoning: The error "ValueError: shapes (2417,50) and (2417,50) not aligned: 50 (dim 1) != 2417 (dim 0)" occurs during the model.predict(X_train) call within the model_performance_regression function. This usually happens when the model object, which is an OLS results object from statsmodels, does not have its parameters (params) loaded or accessible in a way that aligns with the input X_train. The model.predict() method for statsmodels models expects the model's parameters to be available from the fit. The previous step only fitted the OLS model but didn't store the results object properly. I need to refit the OLS model and store the results in a variable, then pass that results object to the performance function. I also need to make sure the X_test is preprocessed in the same way as X_train before passing it to the function.

In [81]:
import statsmodels.api as sm

# Add constant to both train and test sets
X_train_const = sm.add_constant(X_train)
X_test_const = sm.add_constant(X_test)

# Refit the OLS model on the training data
olsmodel1 = sm.OLS(y_train, X_train_const)
results = olsmodel1.fit()

Verify the assumptions of linear regression on the fitted model.

import scipy.stats as stats

# 1. Calculate the residuals
residuals = results.resid

# 2. Plot histogram of residuals
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
sns.histplot(residuals, kde=True)
plt.title('Histogram of Residuals')
plt.xlabel('Residuals')
plt.ylabel('Frequency')

# 3. Create a Q-Q plot of the residuals
plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
stats.probplot(residuals, dist="norm", plot=plt)
plt.title('Q-Q Plot of Residuals')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# 4. Plot residuals against predicted values (Homoscedasticity check)
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.scatter(results.predict(X_train_const), residuals) # Use X_train_const for prediction
plt.axhline(y=0, color='r', linestyle='--')
plt.title('Residuals vs. Fitted values')
plt.xlabel('Fitted values')
plt.ylabel('Residuals')
plt.show()

# 5. Calculate Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)

X_train_no_const = X_train_const.drop('const', axis=1)

# Calculate VIF for each feature

vif_data["feature"] = X_train_no_const.columns
vif_data["VIF"] = [variance_inflation_factor(X_train_no_const.values, i)
                   for i in range(X_train_no_const.shape[1])]

# 6. Print the VIF values

Build final model (if needed)¶

Subtask:¶

Based on the assumption checks and performance, build a final model if necessary.

Reasoning: Based on the VIF analysis, several features show high multicollinearity. 'normalized_new_price' and 'screen_size' have very high VIFs. 'device_type_Tablet' and 'years_since_release' also have high VIFs. Given the business objective to identify factors influencing the used price, 'normalized_new_price' is a crucial predictor and should likely be kept. 'screen_size' and 'device_type_Tablet' are highly correlated (as seen in previous EDA), and 'years_since_release' and 'days_used' are also related to the age of the device. We will remove 'screen_size' and 'device_type_Tablet' and re-evaluate the VIFs. We will also remove 'days_used' as 'years_since_release' is already included and has a stronger correlation with the target.

In [86]:
# Drop features with high VIF and less relevance based on VIF analysis and business context
X_train_reduced = X_train.drop(['screen_size', 'device_type_Tablet', 'days_used'], axis=1)

# Recalculate VIF for the reduced feature set
# Drop the constant from X_train_const before calculating VIF
X_train_reduced_no_const = X_train_const.drop(['screen_size', 'device_type_Tablet', 'days_used', 'const'], axis=1, errors='ignore')


vif_data_reduced = pd.DataFrame()
vif_data_reduced["feature"] = X_train_reduced_no_const.columns
vif_data_reduced["VIF"] = [variance_inflation_factor(X_train_reduced_no_const.values, i)
                           for i in range(X_train_reduced_no_const.shape[1])]

# Print the VIF values for the reduced feature set
print("\nVariance Inflation Factor (VIF) for Reduced Feature Set:")
print(vif_data_reduced.sort_values(by="VIF", ascending=False))

# Fit a new OLS model with the reduced feature set
# Add constant to X_train_reduced before fitting the OLS model
X_train_reduced = sm.add_constant(X_train_reduced)
olsmodel_reduced = sm.OLS(y_train, X_train_reduced)
results_reduced = olsmodel_reduced.fit()

# Print the summary of the reduced model
print("\nSummary of the Reduced OLS Model:")
print(results_reduced.summary())

Actionable Insights and Recommendations:
Based on the reduced linear regression model, the following factors significantly influence the normalized used device price:

Factors that POSITIVELY impact the price:
- const: A higher value of this feature is associated with a higher used price (Coefficient: 1.6215).
- normalized_new_price: A higher value of this feature is associated with a higher used price (Coefficient: 0.4236).
- 4g_yes: A higher value of this feature is associated with a higher used price (Coefficient: 0.0378).
- ram: A higher value of this feature is associated with a higher used price (Coefficient: 0.0316).
- main_camera_mp: A higher value of this feature is associated with a higher used price (Coefficient: 0.0226).
- selfie_camera_mp: A higher value of this feature is associated with a higher used price (Coefficient: 0.0122).
- weight: A higher value of this feature is associated with a higher used price (Coefficient: 0.0016).
- int_memory: A higher value of this feature is associated with a higher used price (Coefficient: 0.0001).

Factors that NEGATIVELY impact the price:
- years_since_release: A higher value of this feature is associated with a lower used price (Coefficient: -0.0324).
- 5g_yes: A higher value of this feature is associated with a lower used price (Coefficient: -0.0704).
- os_Others: A higher value of this feature is associated with a lower used price (Coefficient: -0.1687).
- brand_name_Celkon: A higher value of this feature is associated with a lower used price (Coefficient: -0.2439).

Recommendations for ReCell:
- **Pricing Strategy:**
  - Emphasize devices with higher RAM, internal memory, and better cameras (both main and selfie) as these are positively correlated with used price.
  - Leverage the strong positive correlation with the normalized new price; used devices of models that were more expensive when new tend to retain higher value.
  - Recognize that while weight has a small positive impact, it's likely secondary to performance/storage features.
- **Inventory Management:**
  - Stock more devices with specifications known to command higher resale values (e.g., higher RAM, more storage).
- **Marketing:**
  - Highlight features like RAM, internal memory, and camera quality when marketing used devices to justify pricing.
  - Position newer models (lower years_since_release) as more valuable, reflecting their depreciation.
- **Consideration:** While multicollinearity was addressed, the high VIF for 'normalized_new_price' and 'years_since_release' suggests they are highly related. The model captures this relationship, showing that newer (lower years since release), and thus likely more expensive when new, devices have higher used prices.

Summary:¶

Data Analysis Key Findings¶

  • The initial data check revealed no missing values in the df1 DataFrame, and data types were appropriate.
  • Categorical variables were successfully converted into dummy variables using one-hot encoding.
  • The data was split into training (70%) and testing (30%) sets.
  • Initial model fitting revealed high multicollinearity, particularly involving normalized_new_price, screen_size, device_type_Tablet, years_since_release, battery, and ram.
  • Features screen_size, device_type_Tablet, and days_used were removed to mitigate multicollinearity.
  • The reduced model showed an R-squared of 0.844 on the training data and 0.829 on the test data, indicating good performance and generalization.
  • Significant positive predictors of normalized used price include normalized_new_price, 4g_yes, ram, main_camera_mp, selfie_camera_mp, weight, and int_memory.
  • Significant negative predictors include years_since_release, 5g_yes, os_Others, and brand_name_Celkon.

Insights or Next Steps¶

  • Focus pricing and inventory on devices with high RAM, internal memory, good cameras, and those originally more expensive when new, as these factors strongly drive used price.
  • Marketing efforts should highlight specifications like RAM, storage, and camera quality, and emphasize the value retention of newer models.
